The Challenge

An average cannot tell the whole flavour story

A sensory review needs more than a product ranking. Teams need to see the shape of a profile, the attributes behind a difference, and how price sits alongside those observations.

Hidden signatures

Similar averages can hide very different combinations of fruit, malt, wood, spice and smoke.

Complex comparisons

Looking across many products and attributes makes small but meaningful differences easy to miss.

Price needs context

A price comparison becomes more useful when the sensory dimension is visible beside it.

One shared language

Consistent descriptors and fixed scales help sensory, innovation and commercial teams discuss the same evidence.

HMC Approach

Make the vocabulary consistent. Then make the data visual.

A practical approach for taking a sensory scorecard from the tasting table into a review-ready dashboard.

The Solution

A dashboard you can see, compare and explore

Start with the supplied Power BI screens. Then explore a new sensory lab inspired by their three core questions: what is the profile, how does price compare, and what separates two samples?

Key Takeaways

What a sensory team can take forward

01

Compare the shape

The whole profile explains more than a single average. Keep the attribute vocabulary and scale consistent.

02

Make differences explicit

Pair every overview with an attribute-level comparison so reviewers can explain what changed.

03

Keep the judgement human

Use interactive scenarios to focus the next tasting and discussion. Validate decisions with the sensory team.

Data & methodology

Know what each view represents

Original reference

The three images are the user-supplied dashboards, shown unmodified. Their underlying dataset and rating anchors were not supplied. No new interactive score is presented as a transcription of those screens.

Interactive dataset

Eight fictional coded prototypes, twelve attributes and eight fictional batches demonstrate the interaction. Ratings run from 0 to 5. A higher score means higher intensity; aftertaste represents persistence. A high average is not a quality or preference score. All scenario prices are illustrative INR per 750 mL.

Target fit

The house-style target is synthetic. All attributes have equal weight. RMSE = √[Σ(selected − target)² ÷ 12]. Target fit = 100 × (1 − RMSE ÷ 5), bounded to 0–100. This is a descriptive similarity index, not statistical confidence, a sensory validation result or a quality score.

3D map

X is the mean of Fruity and Floral; Y is the mean of Matured wood and Spices; Z is Peaty/Smoky. Each runs from 0 to 5. The map is a direct three-axis view, not PCA. Distances in this view use three derived coordinates, while target fit uses all twelve attributes. The pale reference marker is the synthetic target.

Blend scenarios

Each blended score and scenario price is the component-weighted average. “Find closest linear mix” scans every integer percentage from 0 to 100 and chooses the lowest profile RMSE. This model does not capture nonlinear sensory interactions, processing, taxes, margins or production costs. Validate an actual formulation through tasting and appropriate formulation work.

Batch review

A batch is flagged when its RMSE exceeds the adjustable limit or any attribute differs from the target by more than 0.50. These are demonstration review rules, not company specifications or validated control limits. Small floating-point differences are excluded at the boundary.

Context and dependencies

The source images define the case-study subject. Publicly available industry material provides general context for sensory analysis and liquid development. The interactive extension does not reproduce or connect to any proprietary company platform. D3 7.9.0 and Three.js r128 are embedded with their licences. The page can run locally without a server.
